title: RIÉ 189, lines 39–52 — ‘Ēzānā of Aksum's vocalized Ge‘ez inscription: the tally of the Nubian campaign, the throne set up at Śadō, and the curse on whoever tears it down. THE FIRST RECORD IN THIS CORPUS IN A LANGUAGE OF SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA.
language_note:
Ge‘ez, the language of the Aksumite kingdom, `gez` as `africa-01-ezana-stone` already declares it for a text it does not carry.

WHAT IS REPRODUCED IS A TRANSLITERATION AND NOT THE ETHIOPIC SCRIPT, AND THE SOURCE SAYS WHY IT IS. Hatke's preface states his practice in his own words: "To these direct quotations I append the original text in transliteration and reserve the use of the original script only in isolated cases for the purpose of clarifying the phonology of certain words and proper names." The vocalized Ge‘ez of RIÉ 189 is one of the quotations he gives in transliteration, so a record built from this page carries a romanisation and not fidal. That is the same position `scandinavia-06-tjurko-bracteate` is in with Elder Futhark, and it is declared for the same reason.

MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED. `ingest.fidelity.classify_original` returns `('transliteration', 'gez', True)` — retrieval eligible — and `english_marker_ratio` on this excerpt is **0.0792**, called on the chunk, against a threshold of 0.18. Record 42's lesson was that the margin is worth knowing before the record is written rather than after `ingest.verify` refuses it; this margin is wide, and it is wide because a hyphen-joined Ge‘ez transliteration shares almost no tokens with English.
date: Mid-fourth century CE. ‘Ēzānā reigned c. 330–370 CE as Hatke dates him, and RIÉ 189 belongs to the part of the reign after the conversion, since it invokes `’ǝgzī’a samāy`, the Lord of Heaven, and not Maḥrem. THE NARROWER DATE IN THE LITERATURE IS A DATE FOR THE CAMPAIGN AND NOT FOR THE CUTTING OF THIS STONE: Hatke dates the second Aksumite invasion of Nubia to 360 on the chronological details and Christological formulae of the GREEK account, RIÉ 271, and this record does not convert that into a date for RIÉ 189.

Za-wahabanī ’Ǝ41.gzī’a samāy ḍēwā ‘ǝd 214 ḍēwā ’anǝst 415 kōna 629. 42.Wa-qǝtla ‘ǝd 602 qǝtla ’anǝst wa-daqīq 156 kōna 743.[58] wa-kōna ḍēwā wa-qǝtl 1387. Wa-mǝhrǝkā lahm 10,544.60 wa-baggǝ‘ 51,050. Wa-’amaḥḍa49.nkū za-manbara za-takalkū la-’ǝgzī’a samāy za-’angaśanī. Wa-la-mǝ50.dr za-yǝṣawwǝrō la-’ǝmma-bō za-naqalō wa-’amāsanō wa-naśatō wǝ’ǝtū wa-51.zamadū yǝśśarraw wa-yǝtnaqqal ’ǝ[m]-bǝḥēr yǝśśarraw. Wa-takalkū za-ma52.nbara ba-hayla ’ǝgzī’a samāy
original_text_note:
Verbatim from George Hatke, `Aksum and Nubia`, §4.5.2.4 'Tallying Up the Spoils of War', at http://dlib.nyu.edu/awdl/isaw/hatke2013-aksum-and-nubia/, read on 2026-09-06. The passage is the transliteration Hatke prints in parentheses immediately after his English translation of the same lines, and his footnote 521 on it reads, in full: `RIE 189 (Bernard et al. 1991: 264-5).`

THE CAPTURE WAS VERIFIED BY HASH AND NOT BY EYE, WHICH IS NEW IN THIS REPOSITORY. The excerpt was typed into a file on the bridge, and the same span was independently sliced out of the live page in the browser; SHA-256 over both, computed on two machines, is `30b926e0d45f8ffd1023c589…` on a length of 852 characters, and the two agree. FINDINGS 48 and 50 are about characters silently changed in transit and FINDING 53 about a text that was not the page; a digest comparison answers all three at once, and it answers them in a way a curator reading the two side by side cannot. It cost about a minute. IT SHOULD BE THE PRACTICE FOR EVERY CAPTURE FROM HERE.

WHAT WAS DROPPED, AND IT IS EXACTLY ONE PAIR OF CHARACTERS. Hatke encloses the whole transliteration in round brackets, because in his page it is a parenthesis inside a sentence. The opening `(` and closing `)` are his sentence's punctuation and not the inscription's, and they are not reproduced. NOTHING ELSE WAS TOUCHED — no line number, no bracket, no diacritic, no space.

THE LINE NUMBERS ARE THE EDITION'S AND ONE OF THEM HAS FALLEN INSIDE A NUMERAL. Hatke prints line divisions as a number and a full stop at the point of division, so `ba-hay45.la` is `ba-ḥayla` divided across lines 44 and 45. In `Wa-mǝhrǝkā lahm 10,544.60` the same convention lands in the middle of the cattle figure: the tally is `10,5` + the line-44 marker + `60`, that is TEN THOUSAND FIVE HUNDRED AND SIXTY cattle, and the string `10,544.60` is a rendering artefact and not a number anyone wrote. THE SAME ARTEFACT IS IN THE ENGLISH, which reads `The booty: 10,544.60 cows`. IT IS NOT REPAIRED IN EITHER FIELD. Repairing it would be editing a published edition on this record's own authority, which is the act FINDING 55 forbids, and the corpus would then hold a figure no source prints. It is quoted, and it is flagged, exactly as the unexplained leading `U ` was on record 43.

AND THE LINE NUMBERS 43 AND 44 ARE THEREFORE NOT VISIBLE AS NUMBERS. 43 does not appear at all in the span and 44 is inside the numeral. This is a property of the page and is recorded so that a reader who counts the markers does not conclude the excerpt is defective.

ONE MORE THING THE SOURCE PRINTS AND THIS RECORD DOES NOT SMOOTH. Hatke marks the pharyngeal in `ḥōrkū` and `’amaḥḍankū` with a dot below, and prints `ba-hayla` twice — at line 44/45 and at line 52 — with a plain `h`. Both spellings are his and both are reproduced. This record makes no claim about which is intended.

THE CAPTURE IS NOT BLIND AND IT IS DECLARED. This session located the source, read the English translation and the transliteration in the same pass, and captured from that reading. There is no independent second reading. Same declaration as records 41, 42 and 43 and as browser pass 1; FINDING 55 applies in full.
reference_translation: 39.And I set up a throne at the confluence of the Nile and 40.Takkazē rivers facing the town of brick which was in the middle of that island. The male prisoners which the L41.ord of Heaven gave me: 214; the female prisoners: 415; the total: 629. 42.The men killed: 602; the women and children killed: 156; the total: 743.[58]. The total of prisoners and dead [together]: 1387. The booty: 10,544.60 cows and 51,050 sheep. And I set up here at Śadō a throne by the pow45.er of the Lord of Heaven, He who aided me and gave me the kingdom. May the L46.ord of Heaven strengthen my kingdom, and as He has on this day defeated for me my enemies 47.may He defeat [them] for me wherever I go, just as He has on this day defeated and subjugated my ene48.mies for me with justice and righteousness, for I do not deal unjustly with people. And I have entrust49.ed this throne which I have set up to the care of the Lord of Heaven who has made me king. And if there be one who removes the earth 50.that supports it and destroys it and tears it down, he and 51.his kinfolk shall be uprooted and eradicated; from the land will he be uprooted. And I have set up this th52.rone through the power of the Lord of Heaven.
reference_translation_note:
Hatke's own English, printed immediately above the transliteration on the same page, captured in the same pass and verified by the same SHA-256 comparison (length 1201).

THE TRANSLATOR IS NAMED AND SAYS SO HIMSELF: "Regarding the use of primary texts in direct quotation, all translations of sources in Ge‘ez, Syriac, and Arabic are my own." This is not an anonymous database field and not an encyclopedia's summary; it is a named scholar's translation in a peer-reviewed monograph, and `seasia-05`'s objection to Wikipedia's Kedukan Bukit English does not reach it.

THE BRACKETS IN THE ENGLISH ARE THE TRANSLATOR'S AND ARE KEPT. `[them]` and `[together]` are his supplements; `743.[58]` carries what appears to be an editorial marker inside the tally, and it is reproduced rather than resolved, because this record does not know what it is. `’ǝ[m]-bǝḥēr` in the transliteration is the same kind of mark on the other side.

WHAT THE ENGLISH SAYS THAT MATTERS TO THIS CORPUS, AND IT IS A NEGATIVE. There is no Rome in it. The connection this record carries is not a word in the text — see `notes`.
translation_source:
George Hatke, `Aksum and Nubia: Warfare, Commerce, and Political Fictions in Ancient Northeast Africa`, Institute for the Study of the Ancient World / NYU Press, 2013, §4.5.2.4, at http://dlib.nyu.edu/awdl/isaw/hatke2013-aksum-and-nubia/. Translation from the Ge‘ez by the author.

THE BOUNDARY OF THE TRANSLATION SEARCH, IN THIS RECORD'S OWN WORDS. What was looked at: this monograph, which prints the transliteration and the English together and cites its own source for the text. What was NOT opened: **Bernand, Drewes and Schneider, `Recueil des inscriptions de l'Éthiopie des périodes pré-axoumite et axoumite`, Tome I: Les documents, Paris 1991** — the edition Hatke's footnote 521 points at for RIÉ 189, at pages 264–5 — and its Tome III of translations and commentary; and **Littmann's `Deutsche Aksum-Expedition` IV (1913)**, which is out of copyright and would carry a German translation. NO CLAIM IS MADE about whether either is reachable, what it costs, or whether its reading differs. The search stopped at the open-access monograph that carries both registers and names the edition behind them.

AND THE SPELLING OF THE EDITORS' NAME IS THE SOURCE'S. Hatke prints `Bernard` throughout — footnote 521, the bibliography entry, and the body — where the RIÉ's editor is Étienne **Bernand**. The citation above gives the name as this record believes it to be and the quotation of the footnote in `original_text_note` gives it as Hatke prints it. Neither is silently corrected into the other.

findspot: Aksum, Tigray, Ethiopia. Hatke introduces RIÉ 189 as "A 52-line inscription in fully vocalized Ge‘ez, RIE 189 from Aksum". THE THRONE THE TEXT DESCRIBES IS NOT THE STONE'S FINDSPOT and the record keeps the two apart: the passage sets up one throne at the confluence of the rivers in Nubia and another `ba-zǝyya ba-Śadō`, here at Śadō, and Hatke's comment on the same passage is that "RIE 189 was thus, like other Aksumite royal inscriptions, erected as part of a symbolic throne. The location of this throne is said to have been a place called Śadō." Where Śadō is, this record does not say.
notes:
F6. **THE LAST PER-REGION FLOOR IN BLOCK F.** Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 3 source-language records against a floor of 4, and — the part the bare count does not show — at `0 local + 2 empire-language from the region + 1 about it`. Its two speaking records were African rulers writing in GREEK. THIS IS THE FIRST TEXT IN THIS CORPUS IN A LANGUAGE OF SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA.

WHY THIS INSCRIPTION AND NOT THE EZANA STONE. See FINDING 80: `africa-01-ezana-stone` holds no Ge‘ez, no Greek and no Sabaean — its `original_text_excerpt` is a bracketed instruction to a later session that `classify_original` calls a `pointer`, and its translation is a titulature quoted from a news website. The handoff documents said the corpus already held the Greek of that stone and it does not. **So the slot was never a second register of a text already held**, and the hunt was free to take any Aksumite royal text in Ge‘ez that a citable open source carries in full.

WHAT THIS RECORD DOES NOT DO, SAID HERE RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER. It does **not** close the answer case `ezana-stone-geez` — "What does the Ge‘ez text of the Ezana Stone say?" RIÉ 189 is a different inscription from the trilingual stone. The case stays failing, and it is now failing for a reason the corpus can state: the corpus has Ge‘ez, and it is not that stone's Ge‘ez.

WHERE THE ROMAN CONNECTION IS, AND IT IS NOT A WORD IN THE TEXT. Nothing in these fourteen lines names Rome. The connection is that **the same king published the same war twice, in two languages, for two readerships** — and it is the GREEK version, RIÉ 271, that is explicitly Christian, invoking the Trinity, while this Ge‘ez one uses the doctrinally neutral `’ǝgzī’a samāy`, the Lord of Heaven. Hatke's §4.5.1 and §4.5.2 are that comparison. The corpus can now hold both sides of the question its own provenance line asks — is the region SPEAKING, or being SPOKEN ABOUT — for one king, one campaign, and one royal genre. `africa-05-adulis-throne` is an Aksumite king's throne inscription in Greek at the Red Sea port where Roman merchants landed; this is an Aksumite king's throne inscription in Ge‘ez at home.

AND THERE IS A SHARPER VERSION OF THE SAME POINT ONE SENTENCE AWAY IN THE SOURCE, NOT TAKEN. Hatke records that ‘Ēzānā's pre-Christian inscriptions call him "son of Maḥrem unconquered by the enemy" (`walda Maḥrǝm za-’ǝy-yǝtmawā’ la-ḍar`) in the Ge‘ez and "son of the invincible god Ares" (`υἱὸς θεoῦ ἀνικήτoυ Ἄρεως`) in the Greek — an Aksumite chancery performing `interpretatio graeca` on its own dynastic god for a Mediterranean readership, and `africa-01`'s translated titulature already carries the Greek half in English. IT WAS NOT TAKEN because the Ge‘ez there is a four-word phrase inside the author's prose, and an excerpt assembled out of parentheticals from three different sentences is the curator's construction and not the source's text. It is written here so that F7 or Block G can find it in one step.

NOT DECLARED GLOSS-CAPABLE. F6 carries **one** `gloss_capable` declaration and ruling 77 spends it on CIH 541; a second is over-delivery that `check_delivery` fails on. The material is nevertheless in the chunked fields if a later tranche wants it: `10,544.60`, which is two numbers and a line break, and `743.[58]`, and `’ǝ[m]-bǝḥēr`.

THE PREDICTION THIS RECORD TESTS. Ruling 78's **P4**, written at `2991e04` before this file existed: FINDING 73 predicts Africa's six ranking pairs degrade as a group; FINDING 79 predicts that only `au-ezana-titles` moves, because the other five expect GREEK chunks and this record contains no Greek at all. Nothing here is gated on it.

THE HUNT'S ONE RECORDED NEGATIVE. **`betamasaheft.eu` is behind a firewall.** Both `https://betamasaheft.eu/` and `https://betamasaheft.eu/inscriptions` returned `403 Access Denied` in a real browser on 2026-09-06, with the page's own text saying "For the moment our website (or the section/page you are trying to access) is behind the firewall. If you would like to use it please send an email to obtain permission." The institutional site `betamasaheft.uni-hamburg.de` is alive and serves news, not data, and the project's GitHub organisation carries no `Inscriptions` repository under that name. This is a REFUSAL TO A BROWSER and not a fetcher being blocked, which is the distinction ruling 76 was made on. Beta maṣāḥǝft was the first of the two leads `F6_CURATION_START.md` named; it is now the first negative recorded against this slot. The second, the printed RIÉ corpus, was not opened and no negative is recorded against it.

findspot_places.note: The findspot as the source gives it — "RIE 189 from Aksum". The id is the one `africa-01-ezana-stone` already resolves against the 2026-08-10 Pleiades snapshot, whose entry describes it as "Present-day Aksum in Ethiopia. The center of the Aksumite Kingdom", feature types 'cultural-landscape, settlement'. IT IS REUSED AND NOT RE-IDENTIFIED: the same ancient place, named the same way by two records, is one gazetteer id.

subject_places.name: The confluence of the Sīdā and the Takkazī
subject_places.note: NO ID. The text places a throne `wǝstēta mahbarta ’aflāg za-Sīdā wa-za-Takkazī`, at the confluence of the rivers Sīdā and Takkazī, which Hatke's English renders 'the confluence of the Nile and Takkazē rivers'. WHICH CONFLUENCE THAT IS, IS A QUESTION THIS RECORD DOES NOT ANSWER — the identification of the Aksumites' Sīdā, and therefore of the meeting point, is a live scholarly question in the source itself, and PHASE2's W1 rule forbids authoring a coordinate for it. `regional` with a note is what an unplaced connection looks like in the placement layer.

subject_places.name: Śadō
subject_places.note: NO ID, AND THE SOURCE IS EXPLICIT THAT IT DOES NOT KNOW EITHER. The text says the king set up a throne `ba-zǝyya ba-Śadō`, here at Śadō, and Hatke says of the same place only that it "was evidently a spot of some importance" because RIÉ 188 was erected there too. Neither the Pleiades snapshot pinned in this repository nor its one GeoNames dump — which is China — carries it, and no coordinate is authored.
